before:
A type annotation gives a variable the declared type. A satisfies expression checks compatibility while retaining the expression's resulting specific type.

Record<Keys, Value> describes object properties: each key named by Keys must have a value compatible with Value. A union of literal keys requires those particular names; Record<string, Value> instead describes string-named properties generally. This is a compile-time type, not a runtime object constructor. A string’s toUpperCase() method returns uppercase text without changing the original string.
satisfies is checked by TypeScript and removed from runtime JavaScript. It does not validate incoming data.
It is not a promise to preserve every literal unchanged. Contextual typing still matters; use precise compiler checks instead of assuming all values remain literal types.

For the exercise, create palette with calm text "mint" and alert tuple [255, 80, 0]. Check it satisfies Record<"calm" | "alert", Paint>, then return the uppercase calm name and the alert's first channel.
